title: Atoms and the cotangent basis at a monoid vertex times a torus
statement:
Let $k$ be a field and $R$ a fine sharp commutative monoid with torsion-free group completion [def-trf-fine-fan-blowup]. Let $A$ be its set of atoms: the nonzero $a\in R$ that cannot be written as a sum of two nonzero elements. Then $A$ is finite and generates $R$ as a monoid. For a finite $t\geq0$, set $B=k[R][y_1^{\pm1},\ldots,y_t^{\pm1}]$ [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization] and let $\mathfrak m=(e^q:q\ne0)+(y_j-1:1\leq j\leq t)$. This is a maximal ideal with residue field $k$. The natural map
$$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\longrightarrow \mathfrak m B_{\mathfrak m}/(\mathfrak m B_{\mathfrak m})^2$$
is an isomorphism of $k$-vector spaces, and the classes of $e^a$ ($a\in A$) together with $y_j-1$ ($1\leq j\leq t$) form a basis of each space. Thus the local cotangent dimension is $|A|+t$. The assertions include $R=\{0\}$, $A=\varnothing$ and $t=0$.

source.place: VIII proof of Lemma 3.2.12(ii), pp.104--105: atoms and vertex cotangent space; minimal-generating-set and square-zero-algebra independence arguments expanded by an agent.

proof.text: Choose a finite generating subset $S\subset R\setminus\{0\}$ of least cardinality, using fineness [def-trf-fine-fan-blowup]. If $s\in S$ were $u+v$ with $u,v\ne0$, express $u,v$ as sums from $S$. If $s$ occurs in the expression for $u$, write $u=s+w$; cancellation in $R\subset R^{\rm gp}$ gives $w+v=0$, contradicting sharpness and $v\ne0$. The same applies to $v$. Thus neither expression contains $s$, so $s$ is generated by $S\setminus\{s\}$, contradicting minimality. Hence every member of $S$ is an atom. Conversely an atom expressed as a sum from $S$ has exactly one summand: two or more summands give two nonzero parts, since a sum of nonzero elements cannot be zero in a sharp monoid. Thus $A=S$, proving finiteness and generation.

source.place: VIII Lemma 3.2.12(ii), pp.104--105: the assertion that indecomposables generate, expanded by a minimal-generating-set argument.

proof.text: Put $z_j=y_j-1$. Sharpness says $q+r=0$ only when $q=r=0$, so the formula $\epsilon(e^q y^n)=0$ for $q\ne0$ and $\epsilon(y^n)=1$, $n\in\mathbf Z^t$, extends by finite sums to a $k$-algebra map $\epsilon:B\to k$; the monomial multiplication is that of [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization]. Its displayed generators all vanish. Conversely $y_j^h-1$ is divisible by $z_j$ for every integer $h$: for $h>0$ use the finite geometric sum, for $h<0$ use $y_j^{-h}(y_j^h-1)=-(y_j^{-h}-1)$, and for $h=0$ it is zero. Telescoping a product gives $y^n-1\in(z_1,\ldots,z_t)$. Every $f\in B$ therefore satisfies $f-\epsilon(f)\in\mathfrak m$, by separating its terms with $q\ne0$. Hence $\ker\epsilon=\mathfrak m$ and $B/\mathfrak m=k$, proving maximality.

source.place: VIII Lemma 3.2.12(ii), p.104: monomial maximal ideal and residue field; Laurent-coordinate augmentation written out.

proof.text: Work modulo $\mathfrak m^2$. If $q\ne0$ is not an atom, write $q=u+v$ with $u,v\ne0$; then $e^q=e^ue^v\in\mathfrak m^2$. For an atom $a$, $e^ay^n\equiv e^a$ since $y^n-1\in\mathfrak m$. The relations $y_j=1+z_j$ and $(1+z_j)(1-z_j)\equiv1$ give $y^n\equiv1+\sum_j n_jz_j$ for all integer exponents, with each integer mapped to $k$. Write $f\in\mathfrak m$ uniquely as a finite sum $\sum_{q,n}c_{q,n}e^qy^n$ using the formal-sum definition [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization]. Since $\sum_n c_{0,n}=\epsilon(f)=0$, its class is $\sum_{a\in A}(\sum_n c_{a,n})[e^a]+\sum_j(\sum_n n_jc_{0,n})[z_j]$. This proves spanning.

source.place: VIII Lemma 3.2.12(ii), pp.104--105: I and I squared decomposed by monomials; explicit Laurent expansion modulo the square.

proof.text: For each atom $a$ define the $k$-linear coefficient functional $C_a(f)=\sum_n c_{a,n}$; define $D_j(f)=\sum_n n_jc_{0,n}$. Finite monomial multiplication [def-trf-monoscheme-toric-realization] gives $C_a(fg)=\epsilon(f)C_a(g)+C_a(f)\epsilon(g)$: the only decompositions of $a$ are $0+a$ and $a+0$. Similarly $D_j(fg)=\epsilon(f)D_j(g)+D_j(f)\epsilon(g)$, since $q+r=0$ forces $q=r=0$ and the $j$-th exponent of $y^{n+m}$ is $n_j+m_j$. These functionals vanish on products of two members of $\mathfrak m$, hence on $\mathfrak m^2$, whose elements are finite sums of such products. On the proposed generators they satisfy $C_a(e^b)=\delta_{ab}$, $C_a(z_j)=0$, $D_j(e^a)=0$, and $D_j(z_i)=\delta_{ji}$. Applying them to a vanishing linear combination proves independence, and with step 3 proves the asserted global basis.

source.place: VIII Lemma 3.2.12(ii), pp.104--105: independence of monomial classes; torus coefficient functionals expanded by the agent.

proof.text: Use the fraction description of $B_{\mathfrak m}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Every member of $\mathfrak mB_{\mathfrak m}$ is $x/s$ with $x\in\mathfrak m$, $s\notin\mathfrak m$, by putting a finite sum over a common denominator. Define $F(x/s)=\epsilon(s)^{-1}[x]\in\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$. To check well-definedness, equality $x/s=x'/s'$ means $u(s'x-sx')=0$ for some $u\notin\mathfrak m$. On $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$, multiplication by any $b\in B$ is multiplication by $\epsilon(b)$, because $b-\epsilon(b)\in\mathfrak m$. Reducing the equality and cancelling the nonzero scalar $\epsilon(u)$ therefore gives $\epsilon(s')[x]=\epsilon(s)[x']$. Common-denominator addition proves that $F$ is $k$-linear. It kills products $(x/s)(x'/s')$ with $x,x'\in\mathfrak m$, and hence the squared localized ideal. The resulting map on the localized cotangent space is inverse to the natural map: one composite sends $[x]$ to $[x]$, while the other uses $x/s-x/\epsilon(s)=x(\epsilon(s)-s)/(s\epsilon(s))\in(\mathfrak mB_{\mathfrak m})^2$. Thus the natural map is the claimed isomorphism.

source.place: Agent expansion of localization at the rational vertex; Stacks algebra.tex Tag 00CO, definition-localization, for the fraction equivalence relation.

proof.text: Transport the basis from steps 3--4 through the isomorphism of step 5. Its index set is the disjoint union of the finite set $A$ and the $t$ torus coordinates, so its cardinality, hence the dimension, is $|A|+t$. If $R=\{0\}$ the minimal generating set and the atom functionals are empty; if $t=0$ the Laurent exponents and torus functionals disappear. When both vanish, $B=k$, $\mathfrak m=0$, and both cotangent spaces are zero. Thus the same arguments include every stated boundary case.

source.place: Conclusion of the preceding explicit calculations; empty monoid and zero torus rank included.
